about: The theory behind the ecosystem, as it applies here: transpilers, clean architecture, dependency injection, state management, retrieval, agents and graphs, tests first, distillation.

rows.title: Theory: what a transpiler is, and why Nuclear goes one way only
rows.summary: A transpiler translates source code of one language into source code of another, instead of machine code. Nuclear's goes only from `.nuc` to the target, so the `.nuc` files are the single source of truth and the generated code is never edited.
body: - A **compiler** turns source into machine code or bytecode. A **transpiler** turns source into the source of another language, which that language's own tools then compile and run. TypeScript to JavaScript is the best known one.
- The gain: the target's ecosystem (its runtime, packages, debugger, stores) is reused whole, and the source language can be as small as its purpose needs.
- **One way only.** Nuclear never reads target code. If both sides could be edited, they would drift apart. With one direction the rule is simple: change the `.nuc`, build again.
- **Declarative.** What changes per target is data (a dialect), not the compiler. The same front end (lexer, parser, resolver) serves every target.
- **Line maps.** The build keeps a map from the generated lines to the `.nuc` lines, so a debugger and a test failure are shown at the Nuclear line.
asks: what is a transpiler
is nuclear compiled or interpreted
why can't I edit the generated code

rows.title: Theory: clean architecture, as Dragonfly applies it
rows.summary: Business rules sit in the middle and depend on nothing outside: a use case is one operation, a repository hides where data comes from, and entry points (a controller, a screen) only call inward. Dragonfly makes these rules kinds, and the compiler enforces them.
body: - **Use case**: one business operation with one entry (`exec`). It knows the rules, not the HTTP route nor the screen that called it. It is the unit that is tested.
- **Repository**: the data of one entity behind an interface of meaningful queries (`byAuthor`, `availableSince`). The use case does not know whether the data comes from a database or another API.
- **Model and entity**: a model is what crosses a boundary, validated; an entity is what is stored.
- **Facade** (`appcomponent`): the one public face of a feature. Others depend on it, never on what is inside, so the inside can change freely.
- **The dependency rule**: calls go inward only: entry point → facade → use case → repository or service.
- **Feature folders** (components): code is grouped by what it does for the business, not by technical layer of the whole app.
Why it matters for an AI agent: every piece is small, has one job and one place. A task can be split into pieces of one file that a small model writes without knowing the rest.

why are there use cases and repositories

what is a facade

rows.title: Theory: dependency injection by type
rows.summary: A declaration does not create what it needs: it names its dependencies as constructor parameters and the framework hands them in, found by their type. In Nuclear that is the header line of a kind; tests ask for an instance with `inject<X>()`.
body: ```nuclear
usecase CreateBook(books: BookRepository, clock: Clock)
exec(input: NewBook) Result<Error, Book>
Ok(~books.save(Book(title = input.title, addedAt = clock.now())))
- The header says what the use case needs; nothing in its body builds a repository.
- The dialect writes the registration in the target's injector. You never write a module or a provider list.
- A test replaces a dependency without touching the code under test (`@mock([Repository])` on mobile and web; an in-memory database on the backend).
- An `appcomponent` has no constructor parameters: it is only aliases to use cases.
asks: how does dependency injection work in nuclear
how do I get a repository inside a use case
what does inject do

rows.title: Theory: state management on mobile and web
rows.summary: A screen does not hold business state: a state manager does. It exposes methods, each method emits a named state (loading, loaded, error), and the screen draws one view per state. In Nuclear the states are a state model and the manager's methods are marked with the state they emit.
body: ```nuclear
// the states of the screen
BooksState
(loaded: Book[], error: BookError, loading: boolean)
@stateModel(BooksState)
statemanager BooksManager
(books: BooksComponent)
load()
@state(BooksState.loading)
loading()
@before(loading)
@state(BooksState.loaded)
load() Result<BookError, Book[]>
~books.all()
- The state model lists the states; a boolean is a state without data.
- A method marked `@state(S.x)` emits that state with what it returns; an `Err` emits the error state.
- The screen uses `<State>Builder` with one callback per state.
- The flow is one way: screen → state manager → facade → use case → repository.
asks: how do I manage state in a mobile app
what is a state manager
how does a screen show loading and error

rows.title: Theory: retrieval (RAG), and why a small model needs it
rows.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation gives a model, at the moment it answers, the few pieces of knowledge its question needs. A small model cannot remember a language it was never trained on, but it can copy a rule and an example placed in front of it. The Smart Graph is that retrieval.
body: - **The limit it solves.** A 3B model knows little about NuclearLang and has a short context window. It cannot read the documentation; it can read five cards.

- **How it is found.** Each card is stored with a vector that represents its meaning. The question becomes a vector too, and the closest cards come back. Exact names in the question (an error code, a command) are matched as well, because meaning alone misses them.

- **What makes retrieval good.** Cards that each answer one question; a title and a summary that say what the card is; the same fact in one place only; links to what is related; nothing the reader must not use (a local agent never sees target-language code).
- **What makes it fail.** Long documents cut at arbitrary places, the same thing said in ten places, text that is about history or plans and not about how to do something.
- **Retrieval is not training.** Nothing in the model changes; the knowledge can be corrected today and is right in the next answer.

how does the agent know nuclear

rows.title: Theory: agents, tools and graphs of steps
rows.summary: An agent is a model that can call tools. Left free, it chooses which tool to call next; in a graph, the steps are fixed and the model only fills each one. Small models follow fixed steps far better than they choose tools, so the local agents are graphs.
body: - **Tool**: a function a model may call, described by its name, parameters and a sentence.
- **Free agent**: the model decides the next tool from the conversation. It needs a strong model: a weak one loops, calls the wrong tool or stops early.

- **Graph of steps**: the program decides the order (recall → write → check → repair); the model writes only the content of a step. Predictable, testable, and each step can have its own prompt and its own small model.

- **Tool executor**: the step between both. The program reads a playbook (a list of steps with their tools) and runs it; the model is asked only where judgment or text is needed: to understand a spec, to write a small piece, to explain a failure.

- **In a backend written in Nuclear**: `tools Name` (each method with a doc comment is a tool), `agent Name(tools: T)` with a `prompt`, and `@state(S) graph Name` whose methods are the nodes (`@start`, `@next("node")`).
asks: what is an agent
what is the difference between an agent and a graph

rows.title: Theory: tests first
rows.summary: Writing the test before the code turns an acceptance criterion into something a machine can check. For an AI agent it is the definition of done: the code is finished when the tests that were written first pass, not when the model says so.
body: - One test per acceptance criterion: the normal case, the edge cases (empty, missing, repeated) and each error the operation can return.
- The test is written from the spec and the plan's names, before the code exists. It may not compile alone; it compiles with the code.
- The code is written until the tests pass. A failing test is evidence, given back to whoever wrote the code.
- A test is never deleted or weakened to make a run pass; a test that is itself wrong is corrected and that is said.
- In the Loop this is the stage *Tests first*, before *Code*, and *Verification* runs them.
asks: why are the tests written first
what is tdd
when is a feature done

rows.title: How the local agents were trained: retrieval and distillation, measured
rows.summary: The local agents were not trained by changing weights. A frontier model answered a bank of tasks once; its answers that pass the compiler became examples in the graph; the local coder is measured against it on tasks whose answers the graph never saw, and every failure is fixed with a general rule or more knowledge.
body: 1. **Reference**: Claude Sonnet answers every task of the bank once, with the same guide and one repair with the compiler's errors.
2. **Distill**: its answers to the *train* tasks that pass become examples in the graph (`solved:` rows). The *test* tasks are held out: their answers never reach the graph.
3. **Local**: the local coder answers every task. An answer passes when `nuclear check` reports no errors and it has every acceptance text.
4. **Study each failure** and fix it with a general rule or more knowledge, never with the answer; then another round.
The bank has 45 tasks: 42 of one file (every backend kind, and the mobile and web platforms) and 3 features of several files; 18 are held out.

Where it stands (round 22): the local 3B coder passes 43 of the 45 tasks, Sonnet 39; every task of one file passes (42 of 42), and 16 of the 18 held-out ones (Sonnet 17). On features of several files written by the local agents alone it passes one or two of three (Sonnet three), which is why the generators and a lead exist.
Measure again after any change to an agent, a prompt or the knowledge: `eval/run.py local`, then `eval/run.py report`.
asks: how were the local agents trained
how good is the local agent
is the local model as good as sonnet
how is the agent evaluated
